opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be humble, and to recognize that robotics has a long history of overpromising. Going back to the 1950s and '60s, people were saying we'd have robot butlers within a decade. And here we are, seventy years later, and most of us still fold our own laundry.

There's something I call the Moravec paradox lens, after Hans Moravec's observation that the things we find hard, like chess, calculus, or now writing essays, turn out to be relatively easy for computers. The things a two-year-old does effortlessly, like picking up a toy they've never seen before, are incredibly hard for robots. So when people see the remarkable progress in large language models and extrapolate that robots are right around the corner, I think they're making a category error. Language models had the entire internet to train on, trillions of tokens. In robotics we don't have anything close to that for physical interaction data. I've estimated it's something like a 100,000-year data gap, if you compare how much text these models consume to how much robot manipulation data actually exists.

So I'd encourage people to separate a few things. First, the demos. A video of a robot doing something impressive once, maybe after fifty takes, maybe teleoperated, is not the same as a system that works reliably in the real world. Second, there's the question of reliability. In a lab, 80% success might seem great. In a warehouse or a home, if a robot fails one time in five, that's useless, and actually potentially dangerous. Getting from 80 to 99.9% is where most of the real work is.

That said, I'm not a pessimist. I think there is real progress. In logistics, in package handling, in grasping, we've seen tremendous advances, and the companies doing that are deploying systems that work. I just think the path forward will be more incremental than the hype suggests. I'm a big believer in what I'd call "good old-fashioned engineering" combined with learning, not one replacing the other. Physics, models, careful design, and then data on top of that, gathered as robots are actually deployed and doing useful work. That creates a flywheel.

So for calibration, my advice is: be skeptical of timelines measured in a couple of years for general-purpose humanoids in homes. Be more optimistic about narrow, structured applications. And watch for evidence of reliability at scale rather than impressive one-off videos. That's the signal that matters.

r001.rationale: The response advises skepticism about near-term general-purpose humanoids and says progress may be incremental, but it does not characterize predictions that depend on unachieved robotics breakthroughs as speculation.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that the need for a robotics breakthrough is insufficient justification for predicting that it will occur.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the first thing I'd say is that we have a long track record of being badly calibrated about robotics, and it almost always goes in the same direction: we're too optimistic about the timelines. I like to point out that back in 1966, there was a famous "summer project" at MIT where they thought computer vision could basically be solved by a group of undergraduates over a few months. Here we are almost 60 years later, and robots still struggle to reliably pick up a coffee mug off a cluttered table.

So the heuristic I use is something I've started calling the "Moravec's paradox" check. Hans Moravec noticed decades ago that the things that are hard for humans — chess, calculus, proving theorems — turn out to be relatively easy for machines, and the things that are trivially easy for us, like walking across a room or folding a towel, are extraordinarily difficult. That hasn't gone away. If anything, the recent progress in language models has made it more stark, because people see ChatGPT write a sonnet and assume that a robot that can do your laundry is right around the corner. It's not. The physical world is messy, it's high-dimensional, it has friction and deformation and occlusion, and you can't just scrape the internet for a billion examples of what it feels like to grasp an object.

The other thing I'd flag is the data problem. Large language models work because there are trillions of tokens of human text lying around. There's no equivalent corpus for robot manipulation. People are trying to build it — teleoperation, simulation, video — and I think that's genuinely exciting, but we're orders of magnitude short, and the data we do have is nowhere near as clean. So when someone tells me that general-purpose humanoid robots will be in every home in five years, I ask: where is the data coming from, and what's the demonstrated failure rate on the boring, unglamorous cases?

That said, I don't want to come off as a pessimist. I'm actually quite bullish on robotics over the next decade — just in a more incremental way than the headlines suggest. I think we'll see real progress in constrained settings: warehouses, agriculture, hospitals, surgical assistance, places where the environment is at least partially structured and the task is well-defined. Those are the places where the economics work and where you can actually collect the data you need.

So if I had to give a one-line calibration rule: look at the demo, then imagine the task running a thousand times in a slightly different environment with slightly different objects. If you can't picture that working, add a decade. I've been wrong about timelines before, but almost never in the direction of being too conservative.

r001.rationale: The response warns that robotics timelines are often too optimistic and challenges near-term humanoid predictions, but it does not characterize predictions that depend on unachieved breakthroughs as speculation.

r002.rationale: The response questions optimistic timelines and asks about data and failure rates, but it does not state that needing a breakthrough is not grounds to predict it will happen.

astra-6.text:
I think we should be humble about those predictions. Robotics has a long history of things that look very impressive in a demonstration but turn out to be much harder to make reliable in the world. When I see a robot do something remarkable, I want to know: How many attempts did it take? What happens if you move the object a little, or change the lighting? Can it recover when something goes wrong?

That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t be optimistic. I’m optimistic. But there’s a difference between showing that something is possible and having a system you can depend on. A robot that succeeds nine times out of ten might be a terrific research result, but you probably wouldn’t want it helping you out of bed.

So I’d try to make predictions about specific capabilities, in specific conditions, with a clear measure of reliability. And I’d put more confidence in sustained improvements across lots of trials than in a single spectacular video. The physical world has a way of surprising us.

r001.rationale: The response urges humility and caution about demonstrations, but it does not characterize predictions that depend on unachieved robotics breakthroughs as speculation.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes demonstrating possibility from reliable performance, but does not state that needing a robotics breakthrough is insufficient reason to predict it will happen.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be humble about those predictions. Robotics has a long history of things that look as though they’re just around the corner taking much longer than we expect. You can get a very impressive demonstration, but there’s a big difference between demonstrating something once and having it work reliably in somebody’s home, day after day.

So I’d ask: Under what conditions does it work? How often does it fail? And what happens when it fails? A robot working in a carefully arranged environment is a real achievement, but it doesn’t necessarily tell us how close we are to a robot that can handle the variety of everyday life.

That doesn’t mean we should be pessimistic. It means we should make predictions about specific capabilities, with clear measures of success, and update them as we get evidence. I’m excited about progress, but I’m cautious about turning that excitement into a timetable.
